newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean defaults on notes reach 15-year high.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean defaults on notes reach 15-year high.

text.p: South Korea's debt default ratio on notes, which hit a 15-year high in April, was an indictment of the reckless expansionism of the country's conglomerates, or "chaebols", analysts said on Thursday.
The ratio of the nation's defaults on notes rose to 0.25 percent in April, compared with 0.15 percent in the same month a year ago and 0.24 percent in March, the Bank of Korea said.
"This is the highest monthly figure in the last 15 years," a central bank official told Reuters.

The bank said the rise was largely due to defaults by affiliate companies of financially troubled groups such as Hanbo, Sammi and Jinro. The notes included such debts as promissory notes and bank cheques.
Analysts said the default statistic revealed the inherent weaknesses of Korean business.
"It is absolute irrefutable proof that the old approach to investment allocation in Korea is grossly inappropriate," said Steve Marvin, research head at Ssangyong Investment Securities.

"The senior management of Korean chaebols invest money with no regard whatsoever for return on that investment. The record default rate tells us that this unscientific approach to investment is no longer viable."

The central bank said 1.89 trillion won worth of notes were not honoured in April out of a total 769.4 trillion won that should have been repaid. The number of defaulting firms rose to 1,318 in April, against 936 a year ago and 1,268 in March.
South Korea has been rocked by a series of corporate failures since early this year, highlighted by the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in January and Sammi Steel Co in March.
A voluntary bank committee set up to keep troubled corporates afloat so far has agreed to bail out six units of the 19th-ranked Jinro Group and four of the Dainong Group.
But the groups have not received any funds yet because their owners have refused to cede management control to creditors as stipulated by the bank committee.
However, analysts said small- and medium-sized companies were suffering the most.
"It's small- and medium-sized companies that bankers permit to go bust," said Henry Morris, managing director at Coryo Securities.
"Bankers don't like to fund small- and medium-sized companies because historically they don't trust the financial information available concerning those companies."
Lee Jung-ja, head of research at HSBC James Capel Securities, said many companies were being sacrificed in South Korea's industrial restructuring.
"South Korea is moving towards heavy industries from light industries because of rising labour costs," she said.
"Some companies fail to conform to the structural changes and go bankrupt."
Analysts said it would take some time before South Korea recovered from the chain reaction of insolvencies.

Morris said the strength of the Japanese yen and smoother wage settlements could boost production and result in higher sales and profits. South Korea competes against Japan in major export items such as semiconductors, cars and ships.
"An improvement in overall business circumstances would mean less pressure on everyone and more available funds to small-and medium-companies," he said.
Marvin at Ssangyong said exports were the key.
"If the economies in Asia or North America slow abruptly then exports will slow, and since the domestic economy is very weak, we could get another series of major bankruptcies."
